title: The Book of Knowledge
hook: the first book: foundations, character, study, idolatry and repentance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides' great code, and your line: the whole law in order. Did you open a code, even for a page? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

A law code is a practical thing. Someone opens it with a question in hand: may I carry this on Shabbat, is this pot still kosher, what do I owe the worker by sundown. So a reader opening Maimonides' code for the first time might expect it to start with something useful. A blessing over bread. The rules of the morning. Instead, the first book of the code is about what a person knows. Who God is. What a good character looks like. Why study matters. What it means to worship something false. How to come back after doing wrong. Only after all that does the code turn to prayer, Shabbat, food and the rest. That opening book has a name of its own.
screen: `A CODE FOR PRACTICAL QUESTIONS.` → `IT DOESN'T START WITH BREAD.` → `IT STARTS WITH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sefer HaMadda. Sefer is book. Madda is knowledge. The Book of Knowledge. Turn it four ways. First, what's inside. Maimonides groups his code into books, and each book into sets of laws. This one holds the laws of the foundations of the Torah, the laws of character, the laws of Torah study, the laws about idolatry, and the laws of repentance. Read that list again and notice the path it walks. Knowing God. Becoming a certain kind of person. Learning. Guarding against false worship. Returning when you fall. Second, the surprise. These are laws. Maimonides writes about knowing God and shaping your temper in the same plain, orderly style he uses elsewhere for damages and contracts. To him, how you think and who you are fall under commandment just as much as what you eat. Third, the order. He could have put this book anywhere. He put it first. The code begins with the inner life, and the outward life of blessings and festivals and courts is built on top of it. Knowing comes before doing. Fourth, the last word of the book. It ends with repentance, teshuvah. So the opening book doesn't only describe the ideal. Before the reader reaches a single rule about Shabbat or food, the code has already explained how to come back from failing. The shape is his choice, and it says something: knowledge first, and a way home already built in.
screen: `BOOK. KNOWLEDGE. THE BOOK OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `INNER LIFE, WRITTEN AS LAW.` · `HE PUT IT FIRST.` · `IT ENDS WITH RETURN.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read its first line. Here it is, in plain English: the foundation of foundations, and the pillar of all wisdom, is to know that there is a First Being. That's all. Tomorrow we open it slowly. Today, just let it be a first line. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Say the line once in your head. Notice which word your mind catches on. Foundation, or pillar, or know, or first. Don't explain it. Just stay near that one word, and come back to it each time you drift. The bell holds the time.
Sefer HaMadda. The Book of Knowledge, the opening book of Maimonides' code, where foundations, character, study, idolatry and repentance come before everything else. Today's word.
Your line: knowledge first. Today, before one ordinary task, pause and ask what it rests on. Why you do it, before how. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Jews who study the Mishneh Torah often begin with the Book of Knowledge, and some study a set portion of the code each day, working through it in order.

fork.setup: you're writing a code of all Jewish law, for ordinary people. where do you put the laws about knowing God and shaping character?
options: at the very end, as an appendix.
at the very beginning, before everything else.
nowhere: a law code is for actions.
fork.reveal: Maimonides put them first, in the Book of Knowledge. the inner life is the foundation, and the rest of the code is built on top of it.

original.note: Hebrew: the book of knowledge, the name of the first book of the Mishneh Torah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a law code starts with practical rules.
what it means: Maimonides opens his code with the Book of Knowledge, about God, character, study, idolatry and return.
what a scholar hears: Sefer HaMadda, where belief and character are written as commandments, and the book closes with Hilkhot Teshuvah.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Sefer HaMadda (contents: Yesodei HaTorah, De'ot, Talmud Torah, Avodah Zarah, Teshuvah)

notes: The first line (Yesodei HaTorah 1:1) is paraphrased in the practice, not quoted; tomorrow's lesson opens it fully.

Editor: cut the unsourced line that readers argued over how a code should open and that critics pushed back (day 1141 already covered the Ra'avad); 'numbered style' became 'orderly style' (halakhah numbering is not Maimonides' own claim); replaced the house-and-furniture image, used on day 1133, and varied the hook's 'Today's word is' closer.
The order of the five sets of laws is given as in the code's list of contents; the number five is not stated aloud.
Hook's examples of practical questions (carrying on Shabbat, kashering a pot, paying a worker by sundown) are illustrations, not claims about where these appear in the code.
